paragraphs: This paper connects structured sparsity in linear regression with robustness to uncertainty. Structured sparsity means encouraging patterns in the fitted coefficients, rather than simply making individual coefficients zero. The authors develop a robust regression model that is equivalent to a broad regularization framework, with group Lasso and fused Lasso included as particular cases.

The equivalence provides another way to understand what these penalties accomplish. A regularization choice can be interpreted through an associated set of possible uncertainties against which the regression model protects itself. Changing that uncertainty set therefore supplies a route to new Lasso-like methods, linking the desired coefficient structure to a robustness formulation.

The authors use this perspective to derive new sparsity results and establish statistical consistency for their proposed regularized regression. Their contribution extends an existing connection between ordinary Lasso and robust regression to more general sparse structures. The stated findings are theoretical: they provide tools for explaining existing algorithms and constructing generalizations through uncertainty modeling.
icml-2013-a-unified-robust-regression-mo.tldr: A robust regression framework explains group and fused Lasso through uncertainty sets and supports new structured sparsity methods.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to predict covariances that change over time in multivariate financial data. Covariance describes how quantities vary together, so its evolution is part of modeling changing market behavior. The authors identify three difficulties with popular approaches: overfitting and multiple local optima, inadequate adaptation to market changes, and substantial computational cost.

Their model addresses these difficulties through a combination of Bayesian estimation, evolving parameters, and particle filtering. The Bayesian approach represents uncertainty instead of relying on a single parameter estimate. A diffusion process lets parameter values change over time, providing the model's mechanism for tracking shifts in market conditions.

Particle filters supply computationally efficient, scalable inference for this evolving model. The authors report excellent performance relative to standard models in experiments with financial data. The contribution is the combination of uncertainty-aware estimation and parameter dynamics in a tractable procedure; the reported comparison supports that combination in the financial datasets studied.
icml-2013-dynamic-covariance-models-for-.tldr: A Bayesian covariance model uses evolving parameters and particle filters to track changing financial relationships efficiently.

paragraphs: Multi-label classification allows one example to have several labels at once. When the available labels number in the hundreds or thousands, learning over the full label space can become computationally expensive. This paper seeks a smaller representation that retains enough of the relationships among labels to support useful predictions.

The method selects a small subset of the original labels that can approximately span the full label space. It uses randomized sampling, with each label's selection probability reflecting its importance among all labels. The central idea is that labels need not all contribute equally to representing the output space, so sampling can concentrate on a more informative subset.

The authors provide theoretical analysis supporting the efficiency of this sampling approach. Experiments on several real-world datasets with many labels also show appealing predictive performance and efficiency. Together, these findings support importance-based label selection as a practical way to reduce computation while retaining an approximate representation of the original prediction problem.
icml-2013-efficient-multi-label-classifi.tldr: Importance-weighted random sampling selects a small set of labels that approximately represents a much larger label space.

paragraphs: Graph-based learning methods often represent relationships between points using Gaussian similarities. Choosing a separate scale for each point lets these similarities adapt to local data density. Entropic affinities choose that scale to achieve a desired perplexity, which can be understood as an effective number of neighbors, but computing these locally adjusted scales is relatively difficult.

The paper studies the mathematical behavior behind this construction. The authors show that entropic affinities implicitly define a continuously differentiable function over the input space and establish bounds for it. They exploit its slowly varying behavior to initialize calculations using either a tree-based or a density-based scheme.

Their numerical algorithm combines those initializations with robustified root-finding methods that converge quickly. The authors describe the resulting computation as nearly optimal and demonstrate greater speed and accuracy than an existing bisection-based approach on image and text data, especially for large datasets. The practical contribution is a more efficient way to compute useful adaptive similarities.
icml-2013-entropic-affinities-properties.tldr: Mathematical properties of entropic affinities enable faster, more accurate computation of locally adaptive similarities.

paragraphs: This paper introduces positive semidefinite tensor factorization, a method that represents a collection of positive semidefinite matrices using fewer basis matrices of the same kind. Each original matrix is expressed as a convex combination of those bases. The authors present this construction as a natural extension of nonnegative matrix factorization for separating sources in mixture signals.

A central modeling problem is deciding how many bases to use. The proposed nonparametric Bayesian model assumes an unlimited collection of potential bases but uses a gamma process to instantiate only a limited number that are needed. This moves the choice of an appropriate basis count into the modeling procedure.

The authors derive a variational Bayesian algorithm with closed-form posterior inference and also provide a multiplicative update rule for maximum-likelihood estimation. Evaluations on synthetic data and real music recordings show the reported superiority of PSDTF. These results support both the matrix-based representation and its use for modeling mixtures without fixing the number of bases in advance.
icml-2013-infinite-positive-semidefinite.tldr: A Bayesian tensor factorization represents mixture signals with positive semidefinite bases while adapting how many bases are used.

paragraphs: This paper targets the cost of making predictions with nonlinear support vector machines while keeping classification accuracy above an acceptable level. Its approach generalizes localized multiple kernel learning to learn an explicit feature representation. That representation is high-dimensional, sparse, and computationally deep, with features organized into a tree.

Classifying in this explicit feature space separates prediction cost from the number of support vectors. The tree structure encodes nonlinear relationships efficiently, and the authors develop optimization routines for learning these structured features. They report scaling the method to problems containing more than half a million training examples.

The abstract describes an exponential prediction speedup over the state of the art. Benchmark experiments report prediction cost reductions exceeding three orders of magnitude in some cases, with a moderate loss of accuracy relative to RBF-SVMs. The method also achieves substantially better accuracy than leading alternatives in the reported comparisons. Its practical significance is the demonstrated tradeoff between prediction speed and retained nonlinear classification accuracy.
icml-2013-local-deep-kernel-learning-for.tldr: Learned tree-structured features greatly reduce nonlinear SVM prediction costs, with a moderate accuracy sacrifice in reported RBF-SVM comparisons.

paragraphs: The paper considers reducing a dataset before choosing a predictive model by empirical risk minimization. Empirical risk minimization selects the hypothesis with the smallest measured training loss. Subsampling can reduce the amount of data involved in that later selection, but the sample must still support a useful final learning decision.

The proposed scheme has an unusual feature: it considers only a subset of the hypotheses that may ultimately be available to the learner. The complete eventual hypothesis set is unknown at sampling time. Despite this mismatch, the authors provide a guarantee that the final excess risk compares favorably with using the entire original dataset.

This result connects an early data reduction decision to the quality of a later learning procedure with a broader hypothesis set. The authors also demonstrate practical benefits by subsampling a large dataset and then fitting boosted trees. The contribution therefore includes both a risk guarantee for subsequent learning and an application showing the usefulness of the sampling scheme.
icml-2013-loss-proportional-subsampling-.tldr: A subsampling scheme provides favorable excess-risk guarantees even when it sees only part of the eventual hypothesis set.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning fits related prediction problems together. This paper approaches that setting by jointly considering two kinds of structure: relationships among tasks and patterns in their residual errors. The task relationships are represented through a covariance matrix, while the residual error matrix describes what remains unexplained by the fitted predictions.

The authors introduce a Matrix Generalized Inverse Gaussian prior and use it to define a Gaussian Matrix Generalized Inverse Gaussian model. This construction provides a low-rank approximation to the task covariance matrix. Combining that model with an assumption about residual error structure produces their proposed regression method for learning multiple tasks.

To make computation tractable, the method combines variational inference with sampling. The paper supplies two sampling strategies for calculating statistics of the MGIG distribution. Experiments report better regression and prediction performance than peer methods. These findings support jointly modeling task covariance and residual structure, with the inference techniques making that combined probabilistic model computationally usable.
icml-2013-multi-task-learning-with-gauss.tldr: A probabilistic multi-task regression model jointly captures low-rank task relationships and structured residual errors.

paragraphs: Video classification often depends on compressing a complex signal into a lower-dimensional representation. The paper argues that common dimensionality reduction methods overlook an important distinction: some information is shared across videos belonging to the same class, while other information is specific to an individual video. Retaining the latter can introduce noise into classification.

Non-Linear Stationary Subspace Analysis explicitly separates these two components. Here, stationary refers to the parts shared across all videos within a class, and non-stationary refers to parts specific to particular videos. The method therefore makes the relationship between variation and class membership central to how the representation is constructed.

The authors demonstrate the approach on action recognition, dynamic texture classification, and scene recognition. These applications provide evidence that separating shared and instance-specific signal components is useful across several video classification tasks. The contribution is a representation-learning approach that accounts for which information persists across a class, rather than treating all retained variation as equally useful for classification.
icml-2013-non-linear-stationary-subspace.tldr: Non-Linear Stationary Subspace Analysis separates class-shared video information from instance-specific variation to improve representations for classification.

paragraphs: Feature encoding with a large, overcomplete dictionary can work well in computer vision, but dictionary size raises a practical question: how much representation is needed for a particular classification accuracy? This paper analyzes that relationship by connecting feature encoding to kernel methods and Nyström sampling, producing bounds that relate accuracy to dictionary size.

The same connection motivates a change in dictionary learning. Dictionaries are often learned from local image patches, but their encoded outputs later pass through a pooling stage. The authors propose learning the dictionary in an end-to-end fashion that takes pooling into account, so the dictionary reflects how its features will ultimately be combined.

Experiments show that the derived bounds can explain observed behavior across multiple datasets. The pooling-aware method also reduces dictionary size by a factor of two for a given accuracy in the reported evaluation. The paper thus links an explanation of the size–accuracy relationship with a concrete way to obtain more compact pooled representations.
icml-2013-on-compact-codes-for-spatially.tldr: Kernel-based analysis explains dictionary size effects, while pooling-aware dictionary learning halves dictionary size at a given accuracy in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Some supervised learning objectives evaluate relationships among examples instead of assigning a separate loss to each example. Ranking and metric learning are examples of this setting. The paper studies how well online stochastic learning methods for such objectives generalize beyond the training data, with particular attention to losses involving pairs of samples.

The authors introduce a general decoupling technique that enables error bounds based on Rademacher complexity, a measure used to characterize the flexibility of a hypothesis class. Their bounds are generally tighter than earlier bounds for the same problem. For strongly convex pairwise losses, the technique also yields fast convergence rates.

The analysis extends to memory-efficient online methods that update using only a bounded subset of previously observed examples. The authors additionally propose an algorithm for higher-order learning problems with bounded regret guarantees. Together, these contributions connect generalization analysis, favorable convergence under strong convexity, and limited-memory learning, addressing both predictive reliability and the storage demands of online relational objectives.
icml-2013-on-the-generalization-ability-.tldr: A decoupling technique strengthens generalization analysis for pairwise online learning and supports guarantees for memory-efficient algorithms.

paragraphs: When one class is much rarer than the other, overall misclassification error can poorly reflect performance on the rare class. This paper studies the arithmetic mean of the true positive and true negative rates, called AM. This measure gives equal weight to correctly recognizing each class, regardless of their relative frequency.

The main question is whether practical learning procedures become optimal for AM as data accumulates. Under mild conditions on the underlying distribution, the authors establish consistency for two approaches: applying an empirically chosen threshold to a suitable class probability estimate, and using an empirically balanced form of risk minimization.

The proofs use balanced losses and results about consistent surrogate objectives for cost-sensitive classification. Experiments support the consistency theorems. The significance is that relatively simple procedures already used in practice receive a theoretical foundation for this particular measure. The guarantee is tied to AM and the stated distributional conditions, rather than extending automatically to every measure used for class imbalance.
icml-2013-on-the-statistical-consistency.tldr: Under mild conditions, thresholding suitable probability estimates and balanced risk minimization are consistent for balanced classification accuracy.

paragraphs: Online kernel learning updates a classifier as examples arrive, while sparse versions try to limit the number of retained support vectors. The paper highlights a difficulty with existing approaches: controlling intermediate classifiers does not necessarily bound the support vectors in the final classifier, which is formed by averaging those intermediate solutions.

The proposed algorithm uses the derivative of a smooth loss function to assess how difficult an example is to classify correctly. A sampling scheme then gives difficult examples a greater chance of becoming support vectors than easy examples. This makes the selection of stored examples responsive to the classifier's learning difficulty.

For smooth loss functions, the analysis gives a performance guarantee similar to standard online learning while using a near-optimal number of support vectors, up to a polynomial factor in the logarithm of the number of steps. Experiments show promising performance against existing sparse online kernel methods. The contribution specifically addresses sparsity of the final averaged solution alongside learning performance.
icml-2013-online-kernel-learning-with-a-.tldr: Difficulty-based sampling gives online kernel learning a near-optimal support-vector bound under a smooth-loss assumption.

paragraphs: Dense random fields connect every pair of variables through pairwise potentials, allowing many direct relationships to influence a prediction. Efficient mean field inference had made these models useful in computer vision, but learning their parameters remained less understood. This paper focuses on estimating parameters in a way that accounts for the inference procedure actually used.

The authors develop an efficient algorithm that estimates all parameters jointly, capturing dependencies among them. They show how to compute gradients efficiently for a variety of loss functions defined over mean field marginals, the approximate individual-variable probabilities produced by inference. Those gradients allow learning to target the quality of the mean field output directly.

As a supporting contribution, the paper presents an efficient dense random field inference algorithm with a convergence guarantee. The two results address complementary needs: parameter learning aligned with approximate inference, and an inference procedure guaranteed to converge. The guarantee concerns convergence of the proposed procedure; the learning contribution concerns optimizing performance through its approximate marginal predictions.
icml-2013-parameter-learning-and-converg.tldr: Joint parameter learning directly optimizes mean field predictions in dense random fields, alongside an efficient convergent inference algorithm.

paragraphs: Learning with label proportions starts from groups of examples whose class proportions are known, while individual labels remain hidden. The paper introduces proportion-SVM to learn from this aggregate supervision. Its objective is to use the group information while explicitly representing the unknown labels that a conventional supervised classifier would normally receive.

The method places those latent labels and the observed proportions within a large-margin framework. The authors emphasize that their approach avoids restrictive assumptions about the data made by existing work. The resulting optimization is a non-convex integer program, reflecting the difficulty of jointly handling unknown discrete labels and the classifier.

To make the problem tractable, the paper proposes two algorithms: one uses alternating optimization, and the other uses a convex relaxation. Extensive experiments on standard datasets show better performance than the state of the art, particularly when groups are larger. These findings support explicitly coupling individual label assignments with group proportions as a useful approach to learning from aggregate labels.
icml-2013-proptosvm-for-learning-with-la.tldr: Proportion-SVM learns a large-margin classifier by jointly modeling hidden individual labels and known group-level class proportions.

paragraphs: Boosted decision trees can make predictions quickly, yet training them can be too slow for applications that need to learn in real time. This paper targets training cost by identifying features that are unlikely to be useful before spending the full effort evaluating them. The approach uses preliminary evidence from a subset of the training data.

The authors prove a bound relating a decision stump's error to its preliminary error on that subset. A decision stump is a simple tree with one split. The bound can be used to prune unpromising features early, and the proposed training algorithm turns this theoretical result into a mechanism for reducing work.

The paper reports speedups of roughly an order of magnitude without reducing final classifier performance. The technique can be combined with existing boosting algorithms and other sampling heuristics, potentially producing further speedups. Its contribution is therefore a way to accelerate training within established boosting procedures through principled early elimination of weak feature candidates.
icml-2013-quickly-boosting-decision-tree.tldr: Error bounds on partial-data evaluations let boosted-tree training prune unpromising features early, yielding reported tenfold speedups without performance loss.

paragraphs: Large kernel and Laplacian matrices occur throughout machine learning and data analysis. This paper revisits randomized ways to approximate such symmetric positive semidefinite matrices with lower-rank representations. The central practical question is how different sampling and projection strategies trade approximation quality against running time across different kinds of matrices.

The authors conduct an empirical evaluation on a diverse collection of these matrices. Their results identify complementary strengths of sampling and projection methods, as well as differences between uniform sampling and nonuniform sampling based on leverage scores. The comparison emphasizes how the choice of randomized approximation strategy affects both computational effort and the resulting approximation.

The paper complements those experiments with worst-case theoretical bounds for random sampling and random projection. These improve earlier guarantees, including additive-error bounds measured by spectral and Frobenius norms and relative-error bounds measured by the trace norm. The contribution combines practical comparisons with stronger mathematical descriptions of approximation error under several distinct ways of measuring it.
icml-2013-revisiting-the-nystrom-method-.tldr: An empirical and theoretical comparison clarifies randomized low-rank matrix approximation and improves several worst-case error bounds.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning when class labels are only partly available or when training and test data come from different sources. It approaches these situations through similarity scores: the learned model expresses how strongly two representations correspond. This provides a framework for using relationships between examples in settings where ordinary labeled training is less straightforward.

The learning problem is formulated as optimizing a fixed-rank bilinear form. Its similarity matrix can be rectangular, which distinguishes the formulation from learning a proper metric. The authors solve the resulting problem using Riemannian optimization, a framework that handles the geometry associated with the constrained matrix representation.

They apply the method to action recognition based on pairs and to object recognition across image domains. The algorithm achieves competitive performance on the benchmark datasets for both applications. These results support fixed-rank similarity learning as a useful approach to partial labels and heterogeneous sources, with the rectangular representation serving as a central feature of the formulation.
icml-2013-riemannian-similarity-learning.tldr: Riemannian optimization learns fixed-rank rectangular similarity matrices for recognition with partial labels or heterogeneous data sources.

paragraphs: Sampling is an important part of analyzing datasets containing billions of records, but constructing the sample must itself remain manageable. The paper introduces ScaSRS, a scalable algorithm for simple random sampling. It makes decisions as records are encountered, using probabilistic thresholds to determine whether each item should be accepted, rejected, or temporarily wait-listed.

These decisions are made independently of other items. The authors prove that, with high probability, the algorithm succeeds and requires storage on the order of the square root of the requested sample size. The approach also extends naturally to stratified sampling, which samples across groups and is useful when the dataset contains heterogeneous populations.

In a MapReduce implementation, the algorithms reduce intermediate output and improve load balancing. These benefits address the distributed computation needed to create samples, in addition to the sampling procedure itself. Evaluations on large datasets demonstrate the reported superiority of the proposed algorithms, supporting their usefulness for sampling at scales where storage and workload distribution matter.
icml-2013-scalable-simple-random-samplin.tldr: ScaSRS uses probabilistic accept, reject, and wait-list decisions to enable scalable random and stratified sampling with low storage requirements.

paragraphs: Denoising autoencoders can clean images by processing small patches and combining the cleaned patches into a larger image. In the usual pipeline, an encoder converts a noisy patch into a latent representation, and a decoder reconstructs a clean patch from that representation. This paper examines a simple modification between those two stages.

The proposed change sparsifies the encoder's latent representation before passing it to the decoder. The stated setting is an autoencoder trained with sparsity regularization, so the intervention builds on a property already encouraged during training. The contribution is an additional operation on the learned representation within the existing patch-denoising pipeline.

Experiments confirm improved denoising both for individual patches and for larger images assembled from those patches. The authors also find improved classification performance when test examples are corrupted by noise. These findings indicate that further sparsifying the representation can help in the studied noisy-input settings, with the denoising claim specifically tied to training that includes sparsity regularization.
icml-2013-simple-sparsification-improves.tldr: Sparsifying latent representations improves denoising in sparsity-regularized autoencoders and also helps classification on noisy test inputs.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a signal from few time-domain samples when the signal is a mixture of a small number of complex multidimensional sinusoids. Their underlying frequencies can vary continuously within the unit disk. A fixed discrete Fourier dictionary can therefore mismatch the true frequencies, creating a difficulty for conventional compressed sensing approaches.

Enhanced matrix completion, or EMaC, addresses this through a structured matrix representation. It converts the data into a low-rank matrix with multi-fold Hankel structure and attempts recovery by minimizing the nuclear norm. The representation uses the signal's sinusoidal structure without requiring frequencies to match a predetermined discrete dictionary.

Under mild incoherence conditions, the authors establish perfect recovery once the sample count exceeds an order of r log² n, where r is the number of sinusoids and n the ambient dimension. They also show near-information-limit completion in many instances, apart from a logarithmic gap. Numerical experiments demonstrate robustness to bounded noise and applicability to super resolution.
icml-2013-spectral-compressed-sensing-vi.tldr: EMaC recovers spectrally sparse signals through structured low-rank matrix completion, with exact-recovery guarantees under incoherence conditions.

paragraphs: Evaluating a policy can involve more than its expected cumulative reward. The variance of that reward describes how much the outcome fluctuates, making it relevant to performance criteria that account for risk. This paper extends temporal difference policy evaluation to include that variability, with finance and process control identified as motivating domains.

The authors propose variants of TD(0) and LSTD(λ) using linear function approximation. This places variance-related evaluation within two temporal difference approaches while representing the quantities being learned through linear approximations. The work concerns assessing a policy through reward criteria that incorporate variance, giving the evaluation a way to describe uncertainty in cumulative outcomes.

The paper proves convergence of the proposed algorithms and demonstrates their utility on a problem with a four-dimensional continuous state space. The theoretical and experimental contributions serve different purposes: convergence supports the learning procedures, while the example shows them operating in a continuous setting. Together, they extend temporal difference evaluation toward risk-sensitive performance assessment.
icml-2013-temporal-difference-methods-fo.tldr: Convergent extensions of TD(0) and LSTD(λ) evaluate reward criteria that include cumulative-reward variance using linear function approximation.

paragraphs: This paper accelerates nearest-neighbor retrieval when database entries are generative models and similarity is measured using KL divergence. Such searches compare probability distributions, including high-dimensional ones. The proposed data structure hierarchically partitions the database and uses a branch-and-bound search strategy to decide which portions deserve further exploration.

The main technical contribution is an efficient decision procedure for exploring nodes during backtracking. It uses a variational approximation to reduce computation at each node, addressing limitations of Bregman Ball Trees on high-dimensional data. The strategy also applies to distributions with hidden state variables and extends beyond regular exponential-family distributions.

Experiments on moderate- and high-dimensional histogram data show substantial speedups over both Bregman Ball Trees and brute-force search. Experiments involving linear dynamical systems further demonstrate applicability to latent-variable models. The findings support a search method whose benefit comes from cheaper decisions within the hierarchy and whose scope includes more complex probability models than simple observed histograms.
icml-2013-that-was-fast-speeding-up-nn-s.tldr: A hierarchical KL-divergence search method uses variational approximations to accelerate retrieval of high-dimensional distributions and latent-variable models.

paragraphs: Topic models discover latent themes in text, but domain-specific applications often require manual checks that those themes correspond to meaningful concepts. This paper introduces a framework for assessing that correspondence at scale. It compares a model's topics with a reference set of domain concepts, making topical relevance something that can be examined systematically.

The framework quantifies four kinds of misalignment: junk, fused, missing, and repeated topics. These categories distinguish irrelevant topics, topics that combine concepts, concepts left uncovered, and redundant topical coverage. Separating these outcomes makes the assessment more informative than treating every failure of correspondence as the same problem.

The analysis compares 10,000 topic model variants against 200 concepts supplied by domain experts. It demonstrates how alignment diagnostics can inform choices of model parameters, inference algorithms, and intrinsic topic-quality measures. The contribution is a structured way to relate model output to domain expectations, allowing large-scale comparisons to reveal how different modeling choices affect conceptual coverage.
icml-2013-topic-model-diagnostics-assess.tldr: Comparing learned topics with expert reference concepts exposes four kinds of misalignment and helps guide topic-model choices.

paragraphs: The paper develops high-probability approximations for two properties of an unknown probability distribution: Bayes error rate and Shannon entropy. Bayes error rate characterizes the best classification error achievable given the underlying distribution. Shannon entropy characterizes uncertainty. Estimating these quantities with guarantees provides information about both prediction difficulty and the distribution's structure.

The Bayes-error approximation makes it possible to construct a classifier whose error approaches the Bayes error rate at a polynomial rate. The entropy approximation supports provable performance guarantees for learning trees and Bayesian networks from continuous variables. Thus, the approximations have consequences for learning procedures as well as for estimating the quantities themselves.

The results depend on regularity conditions on the unknown distributions and cover both bounded and unbounded variables. The title emphasizes two-sided exponential concentration bounds, meaning control of deviations on both sides of the target quantity. The contribution is a set of conditional probabilistic guarantees connecting distributional estimation to classification and learning probabilistic structures from continuous data.
icml-2013-two-sided-exponential-concentr.tldr: Under distributional regularity conditions, high-probability estimates of Bayes error and entropy support guarantees for classification and probabilistic structure learning.
